meta.title: What is an asset under NIS 2? — Inventory in 90 minutes
meta.description: An asset under NIS 2 is anything that processes, stores, or transmits information your operations depend on. Art. 21(2) NIS 2 + CIR 2024/2690 require an inventory; this article shows what counts, how to count, and how to fit it on one page for a 60-person Mittelstand.

nis2Asset.title: What is an asset under NIS 2?
nis2Asset.subtitle: An asset under NIS 2 is anything that processes, stores or transmits information your operations depend on. The directive does not say 'asset' once, but seven of the ten Art. 21(2) measures only make sense once you have the list.

overview.heading: Why the inventory comes first
overview.p1: Most NIS 2 implementations stall in the same place: somebody starts on risk management without first knowing what to assess. The asset inventory is the prerequisite. Without it, risk analysis is guessing, supplier mapping is incomplete, incident response cannot scope, and audits find nothing to test against.
overview.p2: The directive itself does not use the word 'asset' in Art. 21. It talks about 'network and information systems', their security, and the organisation's risk posture. CIR 2024/2690 Art. 2(4) and IT-Grundschutz BSI 200-2 §8.1 fill in the operational meaning: an asset is anything that processes, stores, or transmits information your operations depend on.
overview.p3: For a 60-person Mittelstand the inventory is not a 200-row Excel sheet. It is a one-page list of roughly 10 to 15 grouped entries, which Grundschutz explicitly allows. The point is to have it, keep it current, and let it anchor every other NIS 2 decision.

legalAnchor.heading: Where the duty sits
legalAnchor.description: One operative article, one implementing regulation, one BSI methodology.

directive.label: Art. 21(2)(a) and 21(2)(b) NIS 2
directive.quote: The measures referred to in paragraph 1 shall be based on an all-hazards approach that aims to protect network and information systems and the physical environment of those systems from incidents, and shall include at least the following: (a) policies on risk analysis and information system security; (b) incident handling.
directive.context: Risk analysis and incident handling are listed first, but both require an object to analyse and to handle: the inventory of what you actually have. The directive treats this as a precondition rather than a separate measure.

cir.label: CIR 2024/2690, Art. 2 and Annex II §2.1
cir.quote: The relevant entities shall develop, document and implement policies on risk analysis and information system security, in particular by establishing and maintaining an inventory of their assets including software, hardware, and information.
cir.context: The implementing regulation makes the inventory duty explicit for the entity types it covers (digital service providers). For all other NIS 2 sectors the duty is implicit in Art. 21(2)(a) but Grundschutz makes it operational the same way.

grundschutz.label: BSI IT-Grundschutz BSI 200-2, §8.1
grundschutz.quote: Gleichartige Objekte können zu Gruppen zusammengefasst werden, wenn sie in der Schutzbedarfsfeststellung gleich behandelt werden können.
grundschutz.context: Grouping similar objects is explicitly allowed. A 60-person SME does not need 45 laptop rows; it needs one entry for 'employee laptops, 45 units' if they share the same protection profile. This is what makes the inventory tractable.

whatCounts.heading: What counts as an asset
whatCounts.description: Six categories. Most 60-person Mittelstand entities map cleanly onto 10 to 15 grouped entries across these.

applications.title: Business applications
applications.body: ERP, CRM, accounting, HR, project management, sector-specific software (lab system in pharma, billing platform at a utility, MES on a shop floor). One line per application, even if hosted by a SaaS provider.

data.title: Data stores
data.body: Production databases, file shares, document management, backups, archive systems. Group by sensitivity, not by physical location.

infrastructure.title: Network and compute infrastructure
infrastructure.body: Servers (own or hosted), firewalls, switches, routers, VPN concentrators, identity providers, hypervisors, cloud accounts. One line per cluster of identical purpose.

endpoints.title: Endpoints
endpoints.body: Employee laptops, desktops, mobile devices, tablets. Group by role and OS family. Add separately: privileged admin workstations, kiosks, point-of-sale terminals.

ot.title: OT and physical systems
ot.body: SCADA, PLCs, building management, access control, CCTV, physical access readers, sector-specific industrial control. Often missed; for utilities, manufacturing, hospitals this is the biggest single category.

supplierServices.title: Supplier-provided services
supplierServices.body: Outsourced IT, hosted email, managed firewall, payroll, cloud office, identity-as-a-service. Note the supplier name and the dependency type per Art. 21(2)(d) NIS 2.

grouping.heading: How to group without losing information
grouping.description: Grundschutz BSI 200-2 §8.1 lets you collapse identical assets to a single entry with a count, as long as the protection requirement is the same. Three rules keep the grouping legitimate.

sameProtection.title: Same protection requirement
sameProtection.body: Group 45 employee laptops only if they all share the same Schutzbedarf for confidentiality, integrity and availability. If 5 of them carry payroll data, those 5 are a separate group.

sameRole.title: Same operational role
sameRole.body: Production database server and a developer's sandbox cannot be one group even on identical hardware. Role differs, exposure differs, controls differ.

countedExplicitly.title: Count explicitly
countedExplicitly.body: Write the quantity. '45 employee laptops' tells an auditor scope. '1 cluster of laptops' is useless. The number is the bridge from inventory to risk analysis.

buildInventory.heading: Build the first inventory in 90 minutes
buildInventory.description: Four steps. None of them needs a tool. A spreadsheet, a whiteboard, and one knowledgeable person from IT plus one from operations are enough.

services.title: Step 1 — Start with services delivered (15 min)
services.body: What does your entity actually do for customers? List 3 to 8 core services. For a Stadtwerk: electricity distribution, water distribution, customer billing. Every asset must trace back to a service or it is overhead.

applications.title: Step 2 — Map applications and data to services (25 min)
applications.body: For each service, name the applications it runs on and the data it touches. SAP for billing, the meter-reading platform for distribution, the document archive for legal. One line per application.

infrastructure.title: Step 3 — Drop the infrastructure underneath (25 min)
infrastructure.body: Servers, network, endpoints, identity, cloud accounts. Group ruthlessly per BSI 200-2 §8.1. A 60-person entity rarely exceeds 10 grouped infrastructure rows.

suppliers.title: Step 4 — Add supplier-provided services (25 min)
suppliers.body: Any outsourced service that touches the assets above is itself an asset, plus a supplier dependency. SaaS email is one line; the MSP that manages your firewall is one line. This feeds Art. 21(2)(d) supply chain duties.

pitfalls.heading: Three things that get missed
pitfalls.description: Auditors find the same three holes in almost every first-pass inventory. Cover them now and the second iteration goes faster.

ot.title: OT and building services missing
ot.body: Production lines, building access, CCTV, climate control. Easy to skip because they don't sit on the IT team's desk. Under NIS 2 they are assets the moment they process information related to your service.

dataFlows.title: Data flows not mapped
dataFlows.body: It is not enough to list the applications. Note which data flows from where to where. A payroll file moving from HR system to bank by SFTP is itself a flow that needs protecting.

shadow.title: Shadow IT not surfaced
shadow.body: Departments often run their own SaaS subscriptions (form builders, survey tools, file-sharing). Ask, do not assume. Shadow IT becomes a supplier dependency under Art. 21(2)(d) regardless of who paid for it.

meta.title: What is an ISMS and do I need one for NIS 2?
meta.description: An ISMS is the way an organisation decides, runs and improves its security controls. NIS 2 never names the word ISMS, but Art. 21(2) requires what an ISMS does: documented policy, risk-based decisions, ongoing review.

nis2Isms.title: What is an ISMS and do I need one for NIS 2?
nis2Isms.subtitle: An ISMS is not a piece of software. It is the way your organisation decides on, runs, and improves its security controls. NIS 2 never uses the word, but Art. 21(2) requires exactly what an ISMS does.

overview.heading: Why people get this wrong
overview.p1: ISMS is one of the most misused words in NIS 2 conversations. The most common confusion is treating it as a tool to buy. It is not. An ISMS is the way an organisation manages information security: how policies are decided, how risks are assessed, how controls are picked, how incidents are handled, how all of it is reviewed.
overview.p2: NIS 2 itself never uses 'ISMS' as a term. The directive talks about 'policies', 'measures', 'risk-management', and 'governance'. Art. 21(2) lists ten requirements that together describe exactly what an ISMS does. ISO 27001 calls this same thing 'an information security management system'. IT-Grundschutz calls it an 'Informationssicherheitsmanagementsystem'. The substance is identical.
overview.p3: The practical question is not whether you have an ISMS but how much weight it has. A 60-person Mittelstand running on a one-page policy plus a small risk register plus an annual review meeting can satisfy NIS 2. A 6000-person bank cannot. Both are running an ISMS; one is just heavier than the other.

legalAnchor.heading: Where NIS 2 requires it without naming it
legalAnchor.description: Three textual hooks. Two in the directive, one in IT-Grundschutz that operationalises both.

directive.label: Art. 21(1) and 21(2) NIS 2
directive.quote: Member States shall ensure that essential and important entities take appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures to manage the risks. The measures shall include at least the following: policies on risk analysis and information system security; incident handling; business continuity; supply chain security; security in network and information systems acquisition; policies and procedures to assess the effectiveness of cybersecurity risk-management measures; basic cyber hygiene practices and training; cryptography; human resources security, access control policies and asset management; use of multi-factor authentication.
directive.context: Read together, the ten points describe a management system. 'Policies', 'procedures', 'assess effectiveness' — those are ISMS verbs. NIS 2 does not require ISO 27001 certification, but it requires the substance ISO 27001 covers.

transposition.label: §30 BSIG (German transposition of Art. 21)
transposition.quote: Wesentliche und wichtige Einrichtungen ergreifen geeignete, verhältnismäßige und wirksame technische und organisatorische Maßnahmen, um Störungen der Verfügbarkeit, Integrität und Vertraulichkeit der von ihnen für die Erbringung ihrer Dienste genutzten informationstechnischen Systeme, Komponenten und Prozesse zu vermeiden.
transposition.context: The German transposition uses 'geeignete, verhältnismäßige und wirksame' — appropriate, proportionate and effective. Effective is the word that makes the management system necessary: you can only show effectiveness if you measure and review.

grundschutz.label: BSI IT-Grundschutz BSI 200-1, §3
grundschutz.quote: Ein Informationssicherheitsmanagementsystem (ISMS) ist die Gesamtheit der Regelungen, die zur Steuerung und Überwachung der Aufgaben des Informationssicherheitsmanagements in einer Organisation dienen.
grundschutz.context: The shortest legal definition of an ISMS in German. It is the set of rules that govern how information security is steered and overseen. Not a tool, not a project, not a one-off audit. A way of working.

whatItIs.heading: Four elements that make an ISMS an ISMS
whatItIs.description: Whether you call it ISMS, ISO 27001, IT-Grundschutz or 'our security programme', four elements have to be in place.

scope.title: Defined scope
scope.body: Which parts of the organisation does the ISMS cover, what are the boundaries, what is explicitly out. Without scope, every conversation drifts.

policy.title: Documented policy
policy.body: A written information security policy signed by the management body. One page is enough for a small entity. It commits the organisation to specific principles and assigns responsibility.

riskBased.title: Risk-based decisions
riskBased.body: Controls are chosen because they address identified risks, not because they appear on a checklist. The risk register is the link from inventory to control.

review.title: Periodic review
review.body: At least annually. The management body looks at what worked, what did not, what changed in the threat landscape. A static ISMS is not an ISMS, it is a snapshot.

whatItIsNot.heading: Three things an ISMS is not
whatItIsNot.description: Most procurement-led misunderstandings come from one of these.

notSoftware.title: Not a software tool
notSoftware.body: Tools support an ISMS, they do not replace it. You can run an adequate ISMS in a binder; you cannot replace governance decisions with a SaaS subscription.

notOneTime.title: Not a one-time project
notOneTime.body: Setting up the ISMS is a project. Running it is ongoing work. The annual review is the moment that turns a project deliverable into a system.

notAudit.title: Not the same as an audit
notAudit.body: Audits test whether the ISMS works. They do not constitute the ISMS. An audit without an underlying management system has nothing to test.

doYouNeedOne.heading: Do you need an ISMS for NIS 2?
doYouNeedOne.p1: If your entity is in scope of NIS 2, the substance of an ISMS is required regardless of what you call it. Without a documented policy, risk-based decisions, and a review cycle, you cannot demonstrate that the measures under Art. 21(2) are 'appropriate, proportionate and effective' as §30 BSIG requires.
doYouNeedOne.p2: What is not required is ISO 27001 certification. Many auditors expect it because it is the most-recognised proof, but a self-built ISMS aligned to IT-Grundschutz or a sector standard is equally valid. Choose the standard you can sustain, not the one that looks heaviest on a slide.

buildMinimal.heading: Build a minimal ISMS in four artefacts
buildMinimal.description: Four documents are the absolute floor for a 60-person Mittelstand. Each fits on one page.

scope.title: 1. Scope statement
scope.body: Which legal entities, which sites, which services are covered. One paragraph signed by the management body.

policy.title: 2. Information security policy
policy.body: Five to seven principles. Examples: classify data by sensitivity, restrict admin access to named individuals, train all staff annually, report incidents within agreed timelines, review risks annually.

riskRegister.title: 3. Risk register
riskRegister.body: One row per identified risk. Description, likelihood, impact, treatment decision, owner, review date. Ten to twenty rows for a small entity.

reviewCycle.title: 4. Review schedule
reviewCycle.body: A document that says the management body reviews the ISMS once a year, who attends, what evidence is presented. Without this, the ISMS is decoration.

meta.title: Management body change — transferring NIS 2 responsibility safely
meta.description: When a Geschäftsführer or CEO leaves, the §38 BSIG training duty does not leave with them. Three things have to happen at handover: BSI registry update within 2 weeks, training scheduled, approvals documented.

nis2ManagementChange.title: Management body change — transferring NIS 2 responsibility safely
nis2ManagementChange.subtitle: When the CEO or Geschäftsführer leaves, the §38 BSIG training duty does not go with them. Three things have to happen at handover, or personal liability transfers in the worst way.

overview.heading: Why handover is the most overlooked NIS 2 moment
overview.p1: Most entities prepare for the day NIS 2 first applies to them. Few prepare for the day the person who owns the implementation hands it on. That moment is where §38 BSIG personal liability quietly transfers, where BSI registration data goes stale, and where signed risk acceptances become orphaned.
overview.p2: Under Art. 20 NIS 2 the management body 'can be held liable' for infringements. Liability attaches to the role, not to the person. The incoming Geschäftsführer inherits everything the outgoing one approved, including risks they have never been briefed on. The handover protocol exists to make that briefing happen on the record.
overview.p3: There is no separate NIS 2 handover regulation. The duties come from three places: the §33(5) BSIG 2-week update rule for registration data, the §38 BSIG training duty for the new management body member, and the general Art. 20 NIS 2 approval-and-oversight duty that ports over the moment the new person signs the appointment.

legalAnchor.heading: Three duties that activate on the day of handover
legalAnchor.description: None of them is optional, all three can be missed in the noise of a CEO transition.

directive.label: Art. 20(1) NIS 2 + §38 BSIG (training)
directive.quote: Member States shall ensure that the management bodies of essential and important entities can be held liable for infringements by the entities of Article 21. The members of the management bodies shall be required to follow training in order to gain sufficient knowledge.
directive.context: Liability and training duty attach the day the new management body member is registered, not at a convenient later date. There is no grace period in the directive.

registryUpdate.label: §33(5) BSIG + Art. 27(2) NIS 2 (registry update)
registryUpdate.quote: Wesentliche und wichtige Einrichtungen teilen dem Bundesamt Änderungen der für die Registrierung erforderlichen Angaben innerhalb von zwei Wochen mit.
registryUpdate.context: Two-week deadline. The contact person registered with the BSI is the channel through which incident requests, advisories, and supervisory notices arrive. A stale contact person means BSI inquiries silently fail.

transposition.label: Art. 20(1) NIS 2 (approval continuity)
transposition.quote: The management bodies of essential and important entities shall approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures taken by those entities and shall oversee its implementation.
transposition.context: 'Approve' is a continuing duty. Approvals signed by the outgoing CEO bind the entity, but the incoming CEO becomes accountable for their oversight from day one. They cannot disclaim what they have not been briefed on, so the briefing has to happen at handover.

whatToTransfer.heading: What has to be in the handover pack
whatToTransfer.description: Four artefacts. They exist already if the entity is running an ISMS; the handover just makes them visible to the incoming management body member.

trainingRecord.title: §38 BSIG training records (outgoing)
trainingRecord.body: Proof of completion for the outgoing management body member. The new member's own §38 training has to be arranged separately and promptly.

riskApprovals.title: Signed risk acceptances
riskApprovals.body: Every risk register entry the outgoing CEO accepted (rather than mitigated) is now an obligation the incoming CEO inherits. Review them at handover, do not discover them at audit.

supplierContext.title: Supplier dependency map
supplierContext.body: Which suppliers carry NIS 2 risk under Art. 21(2)(d). The incoming CEO needs to know who they cannot terminate quickly, who holds contractual liability, who is overdue for review.

incidentPlaybook.title: Incident response ownership
incidentPlaybook.body: Who has portal access, who signs off on notifications, who is the designated reporting officer. Names, contact details, escalation chain. This is the document that gets pulled at 03:00 during an incident.

threeSteps.heading: Three steps in the first two weeks
threeSteps.description: The §33(5) BSIG 2-week window dictates the cadence. Treat day 1 of the new management body member as day 1 of the clock.

registryUpdate.title: Step 1 — Update BSI registration
registryUpdate.body: Via the BSI portal under §33(5) BSIG: new contact person, role, contact details. Two weeks from the appointment date. Use the existing ELSTER organisation certificate, that does not change when the management body does.

training.title: Step 2 — Schedule §38 BSIG training
training.body: The new member is required to take cybersecurity risk-management training. No fixed deadline in the BSIG but 'unverzüglich' (without undue delay) under §38(2). Schedule within the first quarter of the new role.

approvals.title: Step 3 — Re-confirm or replace outgoing approvals
approvals.body: Walk the new member through the risk register and the supplier map. Their own signature on whatever they want to keep, a separate decision on whatever they want to revisit. Document the briefing date.

pitfalls.heading: Three things that quietly go wrong
pitfalls.description: All three are silent failures. They surface only when an incident or audit hits.

staleContact.title: BSI contact never updated
staleContact.body: The two-week §33(5) clock runs in the background of a busy transition. Missed update means the BSI's incident contact is a person who no longer works at the entity. Fine exposure under §65 BSIG plus a worst-case incident-notification failure.

unbriefedAcceptances.title: Risk acceptances inherited blindly
unbriefedAcceptances.body: Incoming CEO signs the appointment, by operation of law becomes accountable for risks accepted by the predecessor. Without a briefing they cannot defend the position at audit. The handover briefing is the bridge.

trainingForgotten.title: §38 training scheduled 'later'
trainingForgotten.body: There is no specific deadline, so it slips. Years pass. At the next supervision the BSI asks for proof and there is none. Schedule within the first quarter, not 'when there is time'.

whatHappensIfNotDone.heading: What happens if the handover is informal
whatHappensIfNotDone.p1: Three failure modes compound. First, the BSI registration is stale, so incident-notification reaches no one. Second, the incoming CEO has no briefing on risks they have inherited, so audit defence collapses. Third, the §38 training is missing, which is a separate breach under §38(3) BSIG.
whatHappensIfNotDone.p2: Each of the three triggers the same enforcement path: supervisory notice under Art. 32 NIS 2, possible fine under §65 BSIG, personal exposure of the management body member who signed without checking. None of it is reversible by a retroactive briefing.
